'''Marc R. Wilkins''' is an Australian scientist who is credited with the defining the concept of the [[proteome]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/02648725.1996.10647923 | volume=13 | issue=1 | title=Progress with Proteome Projects: Why All Proteins Expressed by a Genome Should be Identified and How To Do It | year=1996 | journal=Biotechnology and Genetic Engineering Reviews | pages=19–50 | last1 = Wilkins | first1 = Marc R. | last2 = Sanchez | first2 = Jean-Charles | last3 = Gooley | first3 = Andrew A. | last4 = Appel | first4 = Ron D. | last5 = Humphery-Smith | first5 = Ian | last6 = Hochstrasser | first6 = Denis F. | last7 = Williams | first7 = Keith L.| pmid=8948108 | doi-access = free }}</ref>  Wilkins is a professor in the School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences at the [[University of New South Wales]], Sydney.

Wilkins coined the term proteome in 1994 whilst developing the concept as a PhD student at [[Macquarie University]], Sydney, Australia, describing it as the "PROTein complement expressed by a genOME".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilkins |first1=Marc R. |last2=Pasquali |first2=Christian |last3=Appel |first3=Ron D. |last4=Ou |first4=Keli |last5=Golaz |first5=Olivier |last6=Sanchez |first6=Jean-Charles |last7=Yan |first7=Jun X. |last8=Gooley |first8=Andrew. A. |last9=Hughes |first9=Graham |last10=Humphery-Smith |first10=Ian |last11=Williams |first11=Keith L. |last12=Hochstrasser |first12=Denis F. |title=From Proteins to Proteomes: Large Scale Protein Identification by Two-Dimensional Electrophoresis and Amino Acid Analysis |journal=Nature Biotechnology |date=1 January 1996 |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=61–65 |doi=10.1038/nbt0196-61|pmid=9636313 |s2cid=25320181 }}</ref> The term is a generalisation of the concept of the [[genome]] to encompass the set of all proteins that can be produced through the genome through [[alternative splicing]] and [[post-transcriptional modification]] of [[messenger RNA]].<ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/?term=7498152 Wasinger et al. Progress with gene-product mapping of the Mollicutes: Mycoplasma genitalium]</ref>

==Career==
Wilkins held a post-doctoral fellowship from 1995 to 1997 at the [[University of Geneva]], [[Switzerland]], working with Denis Hochstrasser and [[Amos Bairoch|Amos Bairoch]]. He co-developed many of the protein analysis tools available on the [[ExPASy]] web server. He subsequently served as a senior post-doctoral fellow in the Australian Proteome Analysis Facility, which was established by the Australian Government in 1995 as the world's first dedicated proteome research centre.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.proteome.org.au/ |title=APAF - Australian Proteome Research Facility |access-date=17 January 2009 |archive-date=6 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170206184733/http://www.proteome.org.au/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1997 he co-edited the first book on [[proteomics]], ''Proteome Research: New Frontiers in Functional Genomics'' (Wilkins et al. (eds), [[Springer Verlag]]), which sold more than 4,000 copies.<ref>[https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783662034934 Wilkins et al (Eds.) Proteome Research: New Frontiers in Functional Genomics]</ref>

He was a co-founder of the proteomics company Proteome Systems Ltd. It was established in January 1999, and listed on the [[Australian Securities Exchange]] in 2004. Dr Wilkins worked in Proteome Systems full-time for 6 years as leader of its bioinformatics Research and Development team then as Head of Proteomics. It was awarded [[IBM]]'s "Rookie of the Year Award" for companies in the Asia-Pacific region, in 2003. Proteome Systems was renamed Tyrian Diagnostics<ref>"[https://www.proactiveinvestors.com.au/companies/news/146805/tyrian-diagnostics-ltd-in-13m-buyout-of-contango-asset-management-69423.html Tyrian Diagnostics Pty Ltd]"</ref> and ultimately divested its IP. In 2007, Wilkins co-founded the regenerative medicine company, Regeneus.<ref>[http://regeneus.com.au/about/company-summary Regeneus Pty Ltd]</ref> This company has developed treatments for osteoarthritis using adult stem cells, which are now in clinical trials.

Wilkins is currently a professor of Systems Biology at the [[University of New South Wales]],<ref>[https://research.unsw.edu.au/people/professor-marc-wilkins Marc Wilkins - UNSW researcher profile]</ref> and is the director of the Systems Biology Initiative<ref>[http://www.systemsbiology.org.au Systems Biology Initiative]</ref> and the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics.<ref>[http://www.ramaciotti.unsw.edu.au/ Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics]</ref> He has published more than 200 research papers and book chapters.<ref>[https://research.unsw.edu.au/people/professor-marc-wilkins/publications Marc Wilkins - UNSW publication list]</ref> His current research concerns the role of protein methylation in the eukaryotic cell, the use of crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) for proteome-scale analysis of protein interaction networks (the [[interactome]]) and the bioinformatic analysis of next-generation sequencing data. As part of the koala genome consortium, his team did all PacBio long-read sequencing and then Falcon-based assembly to generate the most complete and contiguous marsupial genome to date.<ref>{{cite In 2012, Wilkins was awarded the Australian Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology's Beckman Coulter Discovery Science Award.<ref>[https://www.asbmb.org.au/oldsite/awards/wilkins.html ASBMB Awards]</ref> This prize is awarded to a member for distinguished contributions to the field of biochemistry and molecular biology. The University of New South Wales awarded Wilkins a Doctor of Science (D. Sc.) in 2018.

Recently, he has enjoyed collaborating on the Human Proteome Project ([https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19045-9 published 2020]) and the Human RNA Atlas Project ([https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-021-00936-1 published 2021]).
